title: Guess First
author: Rich Carr
summary: Rich Carr argues that the time spent waiting on an unknown outcome is best used by making a committed, checkable guess. He cites a word-pair study in which people who guessed the missing word, and missed, remembered the full pair better than people who simply studied it, because the attempt activated related memory for the answer to attach to. He then reframes the fear of being wrong: confident errors are corrected more durably than timid guesses, and a private guess on a sticky note carries the benefit without the audience. Carr gives three practical ways to guess well, which are to guess with a reason, to guess the surprising outcome, and to decide in advance what to do on either result. He connects the habit to credibility, since guessing and checking aligns confidence with accuracy, and to AI, where instant answers arrive with no forecast to test them against. The practical takeaway is to spend ten seconds guessing before asking a machine or waiting on news, which builds both memory and judgment.
points: Attempting an answer before seeing it improves memory of the right answer even when the attempt is wrong, because it activates related knowledge for the answer to attach to.
High-confidence errors are corrected more durably than timid guesses, so a wrong guess teaches more than no guess at all.
A private written guess gives the learning benefit of being wrong without social cost and builds a track record of calibrated confidence.
Guess with a reason, guess the surprise, and guess both doors, so that decisions are made calmly during the wait and not in the shock of the answer.
With AI returning answers in seconds, deliberately forming a guess first restores the forecast the answer needs to land on.
quotes: A guess is your best answer, committed before the real one arrives, built from what you already know and held with some sense of how sure you are.
Both groups had the same thirteen seconds, and the guessers spent less of it looking at the answer. They remembered more anyway, both right away and a day and a half later.
When people answer with high confidence and turn out wrong, they fix that answer for good more often than when they guessed timidly.
And the guess I’m asking for is private. It lives on a sticky note, in a notebook, or in the notes app on your phone.
Guess with a reason. Write one sentence on what you think will happen and one on why. The reason matters most, because the reason is what the outcome will grade.
A decision made during the wait gets made with a calm head. A decision made the moment bad news hits gets made by the part of you that just got bad news.
The reply is often right, and it lands in an empty room with no forecast to check it against. An answer needs a guess to land on.
Being confidently wrong in public costs you, and being wrong in private builds the judgment that keeps you from it.
